options.C: The others are using different terminals

questions.rationale: Context that is not committed does not travel, which produces exactly this asymmetry. Hardware (A), repository size (B), and terminal choice (C) do not explain a difference in output quality.

questions.question: A pipeline requires output that always validates against a schema. What is the correct approach?

options.B: Ask for the schema in the prompt and validate afterwards
options.A: Declare the schema as a tool the model must call, and validate on receipt
options.C: Ask for JSON and repair malformed output in code
options.D: Use a lower temperature

questions.rationale: A declared schema makes the structure part of the contract rather than a request, and validation on receipt closes the loop. Prompt requests (B), downstream repair (C), and temperature (D) all leave the shape to chance.

questions.question: Extraction is accurate for common cases and fails on rare formats. What is the most effective response?

options.A: Raise the temperature to encourage flexibility
options.B: Add examples covering the rare formats and define what to return when a field is absent
options.C: Switch to a larger model
options.D: Ask the model to try harder on unusual inputs

questions.rationale: Rare cases fail because they are unspecified, and examples plus an explicit absent-field rule specify them. Temperature (A) adds variance, a larger model (C) is not aimed at the gap, and exhortation (D) is not a specification.

questions.question: What should a schema define for a field the source document may not contain?

options.A: Nothing, since the model will omit it
options.C: An explicit representation for absence, so a missing value is distinguishable from an unfilled one
options.B: A default value that looks plausible
options.D: A free-text field for notes

questions.rationale: Absence must be representable, or downstream code cannot tell a genuine gap from a failure. Silent omission (A) is ambiguous, plausible defaults (B) fabricate data, and a notes field (D) does not make the state machine-readable.

questions.question: Which practice most improves consistency across a long-running structured extraction job?

options.A: Randomising the order of documents
options.D: Fixing the prompt, the schema, and the model version, and recording them with the output
options.B: Increasing the output token limit
options.C: Running each document twice

questions.rationale: Consistency requires that the things that shape output are pinned and recorded, so results remain comparable and reproducible. Ordering (A) is irrelevant, the token cap (B) affects length, and duplicate runs (C) measure variance without removing it.

questions.question: A prompt mixes the instruction, the data, and the output format in continuous prose. What is the first improvement?

options.B: Shorten it
options.A: Separate the sections so the instruction, the input, and the required format are distinguishable
options.C: Move it into the system prompt
options.D: Add emphasis to the format requirement

questions.rationale: Structure lets the model tell instruction from data, which is the most common source of confusion in long prompts. Shortening (B) may remove needed detail, relocation (C) does not clarify, and emphasis (D) does not separate.

questions.question: What is the strongest indicator that a tool surface needs redesign?

options.A: It contains more than ten tools
options.B: The model regularly selects a tool that cannot accomplish the request
options.C: The tools return JSON
options.D: The tools are implemented across several services

questions.rationale: Repeated wrong selection is evidence that the tools are not distinguishable from their descriptions, which is a design fault. Tool count (A), return format (C), and implementation topology (D) are not themselves problems.

questions.question: How should a tool that performs an irreversible action be designed?

options.A: With a description warning the model to be careful
options.C: So that authorisation and confirmation are enforced outside the model
options.B: So that it requires more parameters
options.D: So that it is declared last

questions.rationale: Irreversibility is controlled by the surrounding system, because a prompt-level warning is a request rather than a guarantee. Extra parameters (B) and ordering (D) do not constrain authority.

questions.question: A tool returns a large payload that consumes most of the context window. What is the right change?

options.A: Increase the context window
options.D: Return only what the task needs, with a way to request more detail
options.B: Summarise the payload with a second model call
options.C: Call the tool less often

questions.rationale: Tools should return task-relevant results rather than everything available, which keeps context for reasoning. A larger window (A) postpones the problem, a second call (B) adds cost and a failure point, and calling less often (C) does not change the payload.

questions.question: What belongs in a tool's description?

options.B: The implementation language and framework
options.A: What the tool does, when to use it, and what its parameters mean
options.C: The service level agreement
options.D: The name of the team that owns it

questions.rationale: The description is the model's selection guide, so it must answer purpose, applicability, and parameters. Implementation detail (B), service levels (C), and ownership (D) are irrelevant to the choice.

questions.question: A long agentic run degrades in quality as it proceeds. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The model version changed mid-run
options.B: Context has accumulated until relevant material competes with stale material
options.C: The temperature was set too low
options.D: The tools became slower

questions.rationale: Progressive degradation over a long run is the signature of context accumulation and drift. Versions do not change mid-run (A), low temperature (C) reduces variety rather than quality, and tool latency (D) does not affect correctness.

questions.question: What is the right way to carry state across a compaction boundary?

options.A: Rely on the model to remember what mattered
options.C: Write the decisions and constraints that must persist into an explicit summary that is carried forward
options.B: Increase the context window so compaction is never needed
options.D: Restart the task after compaction

questions.rationale: Persistence must be deliberate, because compaction is lossy by design. Relying on recall (A) is unreliable, a larger window (B) only delays the boundary, and restarting (D) discards the work.

questions.question: Which measure most improves reliability for a workflow that must not silently produce wrong output?

options.A: A larger model
options.D: A validation step that can reject output and trigger a defined fallback
options.B: A longer prompt
options.C: More examples in the prompt

questions.rationale: Reliability against silent failure requires detection and a defined response, which is what validation with a fallback provides. Model size (A), prompt length (B), and examples (C) improve the average case without catching the bad one.

questions.question: What should be measured to know whether a production agentic system is healthy?

options.B: Total tokens consumed
options.A: Task success against a defined criterion, plus the rate and shape of failures
options.C: Average response time
options.D: The number of tool calls per run

questions.rationale: Health is defined by whether the system accomplishes the task and how it fails when it does not. Tokens (B), latency (C), and call counts (D) are cost and behaviour signals that say nothing about correctness.

questions.question: The agent occasionally answers billing questions using an order it looked up three turns earlier for a different customer. What is the architectural fix?

options.A: Increase the context window
options.B: Scope each conversation's context to one customer and clear or isolate prior lookups when the subject changes
options.C: Remove the lookup_order tool
options.D: Instruct the model to be careful about customer identity

questions.rationale: Cross-customer contamination is a context-scoping defect, not a window-size problem

questions.question: process_refund fails intermittently because the billing backend times out. What should the tool return so the agent can behave sensibly?

options.A: An empty string
options.C: A structured error with a category and a retryable flag, so the agent can retry or escalate deliberately
options.B: A message asking the user to try later
options.D: The exception stack trace

questions.rationale: Structured errors with categories and retryable flags are what let an agent recover deliberately

questions.question: Which condition should route a ticket to escalate_to_human rather than continue autonomous resolution?

options.A: The customer writes in a language the agent supports
options.D: The request falls outside documented policy, or the agent cannot make progress after a bounded number of attempts
options.B: The order is more than thirty days old
options.C: The conversation exceeds five turns

questions.rationale: Policy gaps and lack of progress are the documented escalation triggers; turn counts and order age are not

questions.question: The agent sometimes calls get_customer when it should call lookup_order. What is the highest-leverage change?

options.B: Reorder the tools in the configuration
options.A: Rewrite both tool descriptions so each states precisely when it applies and how it differs from the other
options.C: Merge them into one tool with a mode flag
options.D: Increase the model's temperature

questions.rationale: Tool selection runs on descriptions, so differentiation is the fix for confusion between similar tools

questions.question: Backend conventions should apply only when backend files are touched. Where do they belong?

options.A: In the root CLAUDE.md so they are always available
options.B: In a path-scoped rule under .claude/rules/ with frontmatter matching backend paths
options.C: In each engineer's user-level configuration
options.D: In the repository wiki

questions.rationale: Path-scoped rules load conditionally, which is exactly the stated requirement

questions.question: When is plan mode the appropriate choice over direct execution?

options.A: For every change, since planning is always safer
options.C: When the change is large or risky enough that a human should review the approach before edits are made
options.B: Only when the model is unfamiliar with the language
options.D: When the context window is nearly full

questions.rationale: Plan mode is a human review gate for approach, warranted by risk rather than universally

questions.question: A repeated multi-step review procedure should be available to the whole team as a single invocation. What is the right mechanism?

options.A: A shared document describing the steps
options.D: A custom slash command or skill committed to the repository
options.B: A longer CLAUDE.md
options.C: A saved chat transcript

questions.rationale: Repeatable team procedures belong in committed commands or skills, not prose

questions.question: Subagents return full source documents to the coordinator, which then exceeds its context limit. What is the correct design change?

options.B: Give the coordinator a larger model
options.A: Have subagents return structured findings with citations while raw sources stay at the edge or in a scratchpad
options.C: Reduce the number of subagents to one
options.D: Truncate each document to its first page

questions.rationale: Delegation exists to keep bulk at the edge and move distilled results

questions.question: Final reports attribute claims to the wrong sources even though each subagent is individually accurate. What is the likely cause?

options.A: The synthesis model is too small
options.B: The handoff format does not carry claim and source together, so provenance is lost between stages
options.C: The search subagent returns too many results
options.D: Reports are generated before analysis completes

questions.rationale: Provenance survives handoffs only when the format carries claim and source together

questions.question: A subagent fails permanently on one source. What should the coordinator receive?

options.A: Nothing, so the report proceeds
options.C: A propagated error with enough context to decide between retry, exclusion with a noted gap, or abort
options.B: A silent retry loop until it succeeds
options.D: A generic failure flag with no detail

questions.rationale: Errors must propagate with enough context for the coordinator to choose a recovery path

questions.question: The reviewer must emit results a pipeline can parse. Which invocation is correct?

options.A: Interactive session with output redirected to a log
options.D: Non-interactive print mode with JSON output and a schema
options.B: Plan mode with an approval step
options.C: A cron job that emails the transcript

questions.rationale: CI requires non-interactive invocation with structured, schema-validated output

questions.question: Reviews flag many low-value style nits and engineers now ignore them. Which change addresses this?

options.B: Post findings to a separate channel
options.A: Define explicit review criteria and a severity bar in the prompt, with examples of in-scope and out-of-scope findings
options.C: Run the review only on large pull requests
options.D: Cap output at five findings

questions.rationale: Precision comes from explicit criteria and examples that draw the signal boundary

questions.question: Some invoices legitimately lack a delivery date. How should the schema express this?

options.A: Make the field required and let extraction fail
options.B: Make the field nullable so absence is recorded explicitly, with conditional validation where the document type requires it
options.C: Omit the field from the schema
options.D: Default it to today's date

questions.rationale: Nullable fields record legitimate absence; required fields force fabrication or failure

questions.question: Which loop gives the most reliable extraction output?

options.A: Generate, then manually review every record
options.C: Enforce a JSON schema through tool use, validate, and on failure retry with the validation error provided to the model
options.B: Generate three times and take the majority
options.D: Generate with temperature zero and accept the result

questions.rationale: Schema enforcement plus a validation-retry loop is the reliability pattern the guide describes

questions.question: Your team reports 97% accuracy measured only on records that passed validation. Why is that number misleading?

options.A: Accuracy should be measured per field, not per record
options.D: It excludes the failures, so it measures where the system already succeeded rather than the true rate across all documents
options.B: 97% is too low to report
options.C: Validation and accuracy are unrelated

questions.rationale: Measuring only validated records is a biased sample; calibration needs coverage of all documents

questions.question: An internal agent for account managers can read CRM records, draft emails, update opportunities, and delete contacts. Account managers only ever read records and draft emails through it. Under least privilege, what is the right change?

options.A: Log every update and deletion for later audit
options.D: Remove the update and delete capabilities from the agent's configuration entirely
options.B: Add a confirmation dialog before updates and deletions
options.C: Restrict deletions to business hours

questions.rationale: Least privilege removes capabilities the role does not need, eliminating the attack and error surface rather than monitoring it. Logging (A) and confirmations (B) are compensating controls around a privilege that should not exist, and scheduling (C) narrows the window without closing it.

questions.question: After a nightly document refresh, your RAG assistant's answers turned confident but wrong. Model version, prompts, and latency are unchanged. Where do you look first?

options.B: The model, which may have degraded overnight
options.A: The retrieval and indexing layer: whether the refresh broke the index, changed chunking, or introduced mismatched embeddings
options.C: The system prompt wording
options.D: The temperature setting

questions.rationale: The only thing that changed is the document pipeline, and confident-but-wrong is the signature of plausible-but-irrelevant retrieved context. The pinned model (B), unchanged prompt (C), and sampling (D) do not correlate with the refresh.

questions.question: Your platform will expose forty internal capabilities to agents across many teams. Loading all forty tool definitions into every agent's context is bloating prompts and degrading tool selection. What is the architectural remedy?

options.A: Shorter tool descriptions across the board
options.B: Progressive discovery: agents load a small task-relevant toolset, with search or namespacing to pull in others when needed
options.C: One mega-tool with a mode parameter selecting among forty behaviors
options.D: Limit the platform to ten capabilities

questions.rationale: At large tool counts, progressive discovery beats monolithic context: each agent sees what its task needs. Uniformly terser descriptions (A) trade selection quality for tokens, a mode-switch mega-tool (C) hides forty behaviors from the selection mechanism entirely, and capping the platform (D) sacrifices the requirement.

questions.question: A bank wants a system that answers loan officers' policy questions with citations, and separately drafts decline letters from structured decision data. A vendor proposes one autonomous multi-agent system for both. What is the sounder architecture?

options.A: The proposed multi-agent system, since both tasks involve documents
options.C: Two simple components: a retrieval-augmented answer service for policy questions, and a templated generation workflow for letters, each evaluated on its own metrics
options.B: One agent with all tools and a routing prompt
options.D: A single fine-tuned model for both

questions.rationale: Two well-understood problems with different shapes deserve the two cheapest reliable structures, independently testable and governable. Shared document-ness (A) is not an architectural argument, one agent with everything (B) couples unrelated risk profiles, and fine-tuning (D) is the most expensive path to problems retrieval and templates already solve.

questions.question: Your architecture review board asks why you chose a deterministic workflow over an autonomous agent for claims intake. Which justification reflects the tested decision framework?

options.A: Agents are a newer pattern and less proven in general
options.D: The intake path is fully known in advance, so deterministic orchestration is cheaper, auditable, and reliable; autonomy earns its complexity only where the model must choose the path
options.B: Workflows always outperform agents
options.C: The team lacked time to build an agent

questions.rationale: The framework is structural fit: known path, deterministic orchestration; open-ended path, agent. Novelty (A) and universal claims (B) are not engineering arguments, and resourcing (C) justifies a schedule, not an architecture.

questions.question: Legal review quality is subjective, and your team disagrees about whether the assistant's clause summaries are "good." What makes evaluation tractable?

options.B: Ship and count complaints
options.A: Define a rubric with the failure modes that matter, build a labeled evaluation set with counsel, and combine rubric-based model grading with periodic human review
options.C: Exact string match against one reference summary per clause
options.D: Grade outputs by length

questions.rationale: Subjective quality becomes measurable through rubrics, labeled sets, and mixed methodology with humans anchoring the judgment. Complaint-counting (B) measures too late, exact match (C) fails every valid paraphrase, and length (D) measures nothing.

questions.question: A prompt change looks better in demos. Before rolling it to all users, what is the disciplined path?

options.A: Roll it out; demos are representative
options.B: Run it against the regression evaluation set, then A/B it against the current prompt on real traffic with predefined metrics before full rollout
options.C: Ask the team to vote
options.D: Roll out to everyone with a feedback banner

questions.rationale: Changes to prompts are production changes: regression evaluation catches breakage, and an A/B on defined metrics establishes improvement before exposure. Demos (A) and votes (C) are anecdotes, and full rollout with a banner (D) is the experiment without the control.

questions.question: A healthcare client requires that no protected health information reach the model provider, while clinicians want free-text queries about patients. Which design meets both?

options.A: Trust clinicians to avoid typing identifiers
options.C: A de-identification layer that strips or tokenizes PHI before the API call, re-associating results locally, with logging and periodic audits of the boundary
options.B: A system prompt instructing the model to forget PHI
options.D: Blocking free-text queries entirely

questions.rationale: Compliance boundaries are enforced by architecture: PHI is removed before it crosses, and the control is auditable. Trust (A) is not a control, model instructions (B) act after the data already crossed, and a hard block (D) fails the stated business need that a compliant design can meet.

questions.question: Your Claude solution's executive sponsor asks for "99.9% accuracy or we cancel." Accuracy on the task plateaus near 92% with human review catching the rest. What is the architect's correct move?

options.A: Promise 99.9% and hope model upgrades close the gap
options.D: Reframe the target around the end-to-end process: the system plus confidence-routed human review achieves the business outcome, with measured rates, costs, and the tradeoff curve made explicit
options.B: Decline to discuss numbers with non-engineers
options.C: Quietly redefine accuracy so the number reads higher

questions.rationale: Managing expectations with explicit, honest tradeoffs is scored material at this level: the deliverable is the business outcome of the whole pipeline, not a raw model metric. Overpromising (A), stonewalling (B), and metric games (C) each destroy the trust the role exists to build.

questions.question: Three teams configure Claude Code independently: conventions drift, and new engineers take days to become productive. What is the enablement fix?

options.B: Mandate that engineers memorize the conventions
options.A: Ship a shared baseline: version-controlled team configuration, common skills and commands, and an onboarding path, with team-specific rules layered on top
options.C: Prohibit Claude Code until conventions settle
options.D: Let each engineer keep personal settings only

questions.rationale: Team-level enablement means shared, versioned configuration with local extension, which is what makes tooling productive at organizational scale. Memorization (B) does not configure anything, prohibition (C) discards the productivity the domain exists to deliver, and personal-only settings (D) is the drift you started with.

questions.question: A customer requires that no request data leave their AWS account. Which deployment satisfies the constraint?

options.A: The Claude API with a signed data processing agreement
options.B: Claude through Amazon Bedrock within the customer's own account and region
options.C: The Claude API with request logging disabled
options.D: Any deployment, provided the data is encrypted in transit

questions.rationale: A residency constraint of this kind is met by running within the customer's own cloud boundary, which is what Bedrock provides. A contractual agreement (A), disabled logging (C), and transport encryption (D) all still involve the data leaving the account.

questions.question: An enterprise standardised on Google Cloud and requires identity, billing, and audit to run through existing controls. What follows?

options.A: Deploy on Bedrock for feature parity
options.C: Deploy through Vertex AI so the platform's identity, billing, and audit apply
options.B: Use the Claude API and replicate the controls
options.D: Let each team choose its own path

questions.rationale: Aligning with the platform the enterprise already governs is what makes existing controls apply without duplication. A different cloud (A) creates a second control plane, replication (B) is expensive and drifts, and per-team choice (D) removes governance.

questions.question: A design places Claude behind an internal service that every application calls. What is the principal benefit?

options.A: It reduces token cost
options.D: Authentication, rate limiting, logging, and model routing are enforced in one place
options.B: It removes the need for evaluation
options.C: It guarantees lower latency

questions.rationale: A single integration point is where cross-cutting concerns can be applied consistently and changed once. It does not reduce token cost (A) or remove the need to evaluate (B), and an extra hop generally adds latency (C).

questions.question: A legacy system can only call synchronous endpoints with a two-second timeout, but the task needs long reasoning. What is the appropriate design?

options.B: Force the model to answer within two seconds
options.A: Accept the request, return an identifier immediately, and deliver the result asynchronously
options.C: Increase the legacy timeout
options.D: Use the smallest model available

questions.rationale: Decoupling submission from delivery lets the constraint and the workload coexist without degrading either. Truncating the reasoning (B, D) sacrifices the task, and changing the legacy system (C) is usually the constraint rather than an option.

questions.question: What is the most important consideration when a solution must run across two clouds?

options.A: Using identical prompts in both
options.B: Establishing which behaviours must be identical and evaluating for those on each platform
options.C: Choosing the cheaper platform for both
options.D: Deploying to whichever region is nearest

questions.rationale: Cross-platform equivalence is a requirement to be defined and then verified, not assumed. Identical prompts (A) do not guarantee identical behaviour, and cost (C) and proximity (D) do not address consistency.

questions.question: A stakeholder asks for an autonomous agent to handle an end-to-end financial approval process. What should the architect establish first?

options.A: Which model to use
options.C: Which decisions carry accountability and must remain with a person
options.B: The expected token cost
options.D: Whether the agent can be built in the available time

questions.rationale: Where accountability sits determines the shape of the solution and what may be automated at all. Model choice (A), cost (B), and schedule (D) are all downstream of that boundary.

questions.question: Two designs meet the functional requirement. One is simpler and slightly less capable. What should decide?

options.A: The more capable design, since capability is the point
options.D: Whether the extra capability is needed by a stated requirement, weighed against the cost of complexity
options.B: The design the team finds more interesting
options.C: The design with more components, for future flexibility

questions.rationale: Complexity is a cost paid continuously in operation and maintenance, so it must be bought by a real requirement. Capability for its own sake (A), preference (B), and speculative flexibility (C) all pay that cost without justification.

questions.question: A proposed architecture depends on the model behaving correctly for a control that regulation requires. What is the correct judgment?

options.B: Acceptable if evaluation shows high accuracy
options.A: Unacceptable: a required control must be enforced deterministically outside the model
options.C: Acceptable with a disclaimer to the regulator
options.D: Acceptable if a larger model is used

questions.rationale: A regulatory control needs a guarantee, and probabilistic behaviour cannot supply one however high the measured accuracy. Accuracy (B), disclosure (C), and model size (D) do not convert a tendency into a guarantee.

questions.question: What is the clearest sign that a solution has been over-engineered?

options.A: It uses more than one model
options.B: Components exist that no stated requirement depends on
options.C: It has an evaluation suite
options.D: It includes a human approval step

questions.rationale: Unjustified components are the definition of over-engineering and are the parts that will rot. Multiple models (A), evaluation (C), and approval steps (D) are all defensible when a requirement calls for them.

questions.question: What must exist before a solution can be said to be ready for production?

options.A: A demonstration that impressed stakeholders
options.C: A defined success criterion and measured performance against representative data
options.B: Agreement from the engineering team
options.D: A completed cost estimate

questions.rationale: Readiness is a measured claim against a stated bar, which is what distinguishes it from an impression. Demonstrations (A), consensus (B), and cost (D) do not establish whether the system works.

questions.question: An evaluation set is drawn entirely from cases the system already handles well. What is the consequence?

options.A: It gives a reliable measure of quality
options.D: It overstates performance and hides the failure modes that matter
options.B: It is acceptable if it is large enough
options.C: It only matters for regulated systems

questions.rationale: An unrepresentative set measures the wrong distribution, and size cannot correct a biased sample. It is not reliable (A), scale does not fix bias (B), and the problem is universal rather than sector-specific (C).

questions.question: A prompt change improves the target metric but degrades an unmeasured behaviour. How is this best prevented?

options.B: Changing one thing at a time
options.A: Maintaining a regression suite that covers behaviours the system must not lose
options.C: Reviewing changes more carefully
options.D: Limiting how often prompts change

questions.rationale: Silent regressions are caught by explicitly testing what must not break. Single changes (B) and careful review (C) reduce risk without detecting it, and slowing change (D) does not make it safe.

questions.question: What should trigger re-evaluation of a deployed solution?

options.A: Only a reported incident
options.B: A change to the model, the prompt, the data distribution, or the requirement
options.C: A fixed annual schedule
options.D: A change in cost

questions.rationale: Any change to the things that determine behaviour invalidates prior measurement. Waiting for incidents (A) detects late, a fixed schedule (C) is unrelated to actual change, and cost (D) does not affect correctness.

questions.question: How should an architect treat a request to log full prompts and responses for audit?

options.A: Implement it, since audit requirements take precedence
options.C: Establish what the audit actually requires, since prompts and responses may contain personal or confidential data
options.B: Refuse, since logging creates risk
options.D: Log responses only

questions.rationale: Audit and data protection are both real constraints, and the design must satisfy the audit purpose without retaining more than is warranted. Blanket implementation (A) and blanket refusal (B) ignore one side, and a partial rule (D) is arbitrary without knowing the requirement.

questions.question: What is the correct treatment of content retrieved from an untrusted source before it reaches the model?

options.A: It is safe once scanned for known attack strings
options.D: It is untrusted data throughout, and the model's authority must be bounded regardless of its content
options.B: It is safe if the model is instructed to disregard instructions within it
options.C: It is safe if it comes over an encrypted channel

questions.rationale: The durable control is that the model cannot exceed its permissions whatever the content persuades it to attempt. String scanning (A) and prompt instructions (B) are bypassable, and transport security (C) says nothing about the content.

questions.question: Who is accountable for a wrong decision produced by an automated Claude workflow?

options.B: The model provider
options.A: The organisation that deployed the workflow
options.C: The engineer who wrote the prompt
options.D: Nobody, since the output was automated

questions.rationale: Deploying an automated decision means owning its outcomes, which is why the boundaries of automation are an architectural decision. The provider (B) supplies a capability, individual authorship (C) does not transfer organisational responsibility, and automation does not remove accountability (D).

questions.question: An executive sponsor asks for a single number showing how good the solution is. What is the right response?

options.A: Provide the headline accuracy figure
options.B: Provide the measure that matches the decision they face, with its limits stated
options.C: Explain that quality cannot be summarised
options.D: Provide the model's benchmark score

questions.rationale: A useful metric is one tied to the decision at hand and honest about what it does not cover. A bare accuracy figure (A) and a benchmark score (D) can mislead, and refusing to summarise (C) fails the sponsor.

questions.question: A pilot succeeded with ten users and the business wants to roll out to two thousand. What should the architect raise first?

options.A: The cost of additional licences
options.C: Which assumptions held at ten users and may not hold at two thousand
options.B: The need for a larger model
options.D: The training schedule

questions.rationale: Scale invalidates assumptions about inputs, support, and edge cases, and naming those is the architect's contribution. Licences (A), model size (B), and training (D) are downstream of knowing what breaks.

questions.question: What most reduces the risk that a delivered solution decays after handover?

options.A: Comprehensive documentation at delivery
options.D: A named owner with a defined routine for evaluation, monitoring, and update
options.B: A longer warranty period
options.C: Training every user

questions.rationale: Decay is prevented by ongoing ownership and a routine, not by artefacts produced once. Documentation (A) and training (C) age, and a warranty (B) covers defects rather than drift.

questions.question: How should an architect choose a model for a solution with several different tasks?

options.B: One model for everything, for simplicity
options.A: Match each task to the smallest model that meets its requirement, and evaluate the choices
options.C: The largest model for everything, for safety
options.D: The newest model for everything

questions.rationale: Different tasks have different requirements, and matching each keeps cost proportionate while evidence supports the choice. Uniform choices (B, C, D) optimise for convenience rather than fit.

questions.question: What is the correct treatment of the context window in a production design?

options.A: A capacity to fill as fully as possible
options.B: A budget to allocate deliberately between instructions, retrieved material, and working state
options.C: A limit that only matters for long documents
options.D: A setting to raise when quality drops

questions.rationale: Context is a scarce resource whose allocation determines quality, so it is designed rather than consumed. Filling it (A) invites dilution, it matters well beyond long documents (C), and enlarging it (D) does not fix an allocation problem.

questions.question: A solution's prompts are maintained by three teams and have diverged. What is the appropriate remedy?

options.A: Appoint one team to own all prompting
options.C: Version the prompts as artefacts with defined ownership, review, and evaluation on change
options.B: Freeze the prompts
options.D: Move all prompts into the system prompt

questions.rationale: Prompts that determine production behaviour deserve the same lifecycle as code. Centralising ownership (A) may not fit the organisation, freezing (B) blocks improvement, and relocation (D) does not address governance.

questions.question: An organisation wants consistent Claude Code practice across many repositories. What is the most durable approach?

options.A: A written policy circulated by email
options.D: Committed project memory and shared skills in each repository, reviewed like code
options.B: A one-off training session
options.C: Requiring approval for each use

questions.rationale: Conventions travel when they live in the repository and are reviewed with the work. Policies (A) and training (B) fade, and per-use approval (C) creates friction without conveying practice.

questions.question: What is the most useful measure of whether a developer enablement programme is working?

options.B: The number of people trained
options.A: Change in the outcomes the tooling was adopted to improve
options.C: Licence utilisation
options.D: The volume of tool calls

questions.rationale: Enablement is justified by the outcome it moves, which is what should be measured. Attendance (B), utilisation (C), and activity (D) measure uptake rather than benefit.

questions.question: A team reports that Claude Code helps with new code but hurts on a legacy service. What should the architect investigate?

options.A: Whether the team needs more training
options.B: Whether the legacy service lacks the committed context and conventions the model needs
options.C: Whether a larger model would help
options.D: Whether the legacy service should be rewritten

questions.rationale: A difference between codebases usually reflects a difference in the context available in each. Training (A) does not supply repository context, a larger model (C) cannot infer undocumented conventions, and a rewrite (D) is a disproportionate response to a diagnosis not yet made.

questions.question: A retailer wants Claude to answer product questions from a 40,000-document catalogue that changes daily. Which architecture fits?

options.A: Fine-tune a model on the catalogue nightly
options.C: Retrieval over an index refreshed as the catalogue changes, with the model answering from retrieved context
options.B: Load the catalogue into the system prompt
options.D: An autonomous agent that browses the public website

questions.rationale: Frequently changing knowledge belongs in retrieval, not in weights or a context window

questions.question: After a re-index, your retrieval system returns semantically similar but commercially wrong products. Which investigation comes first?

options.A: The generation prompt
options.D: Chunking and embedding configuration, and whether the index was rebuilt consistently
options.B: The model version
options.C: The user interface

questions.rationale: Degradation following a re-index points at chunking, embeddings, and index consistency

questions.question: An agent used by 300 employees exposes 45 tools across eight systems. Selection quality is degrading. What is the architectural response?

options.B: Shorten all tool descriptions
options.A: Scope toolsets per task or role, with progressive discovery for the rest
options.C: Merge tools into a few multi-mode tools
options.D: Replace the agent with a larger model

questions.rationale: At large tool counts, scoping and progressive discovery preserve selection quality

questions.question: Which evaluation design best fits a summarization feature where quality is subjective?

options.A: Exact match against reference summaries
options.B: A rubric covering the failure modes that matter, applied by model graders and periodically audited by humans on a labeled set
options.C: Average output length compared to references
options.D: User thumbs-up counts alone

questions.rationale: Subjective quality becomes measurable through rubrics, labeled sets, and mixed methodology

questions.question: Before a prompt change reaches all users, what is the disciplined sequence?

options.A: Ship it and monitor complaints
options.C: Regression evaluation, then a controlled A/B against the current prompt on predefined metrics, then rollout
options.B: Team vote followed by rollout
options.D: Rollout with a feedback form

questions.rationale: Prompt changes are production changes: regression first, then a controlled comparison

questions.question: A hospital system requires that protected health information never reach the model provider, while clinicians need free-text search. Which design satisfies both?

options.A: A policy instructing clinicians not to type identifiers
options.D: A de-identification layer that removes or tokenizes PHI before the call, with local re-association and auditing
options.B: A system prompt instructing the model to disregard PHI
options.C: Restricting the feature to structured queries only

questions.rationale: Compliance boundaries are enforced architecturally before data crosses, and audited

questions.question: Which is the correct application of human-in-the-loop review at scale?

options.B: Review every output regardless of risk
options.A: Route by confidence and consequence, so low-confidence and high-impact cases reach humans while routine cases flow through
options.C: Review a fixed 10% sample chosen at random
options.D: Review only what users complain about

questions.rationale: Confidence and consequence routing makes human review affordable and effective

questions.question: An executive sponsor demands a single accuracy number for a system whose performance varies sharply by document type. What does a competent architect present?

options.A: The highest observed number
options.B: Performance broken out by document type with the aggregate, the measurement method, and what the business outcome is after human review
options.C: A refusal to quantify
options.D: An average weighted to look favorable

questions.rationale: Honest segmentation plus method and end-to-end outcome is what earns and keeps trust

questions.question: Your design must satisfy GDPR for EU customer data. Which requirement most directly shapes the architecture?

options.A: Response latency targets
options.C: Data minimization, purpose limitation, and the ability to delete personal data on request
options.B: The choice of programming language
options.D: The number of model providers

questions.rationale: GDPR drives minimization, purpose limitation, and erasure, all of which shape design

questions.question: Which is the correct reason to prefer a workflow over an agent for a document intake process?

options.A: Workflows are always more accurate
options.D: The processing path is known in advance, so deterministic orchestration is cheaper, testable, and auditable
options.B: Agents cannot process documents
options.C: Workflows use less context

questions.rationale: Known path, deterministic orchestration; autonomy earns its complexity only when the path is not known

questions.question: An application sends an identical 12,000-token policy preamble on every request. Which optimization addresses both latency and cost?

options.B: Splitting the preamble across two requests
options.A: Ordering the static preamble first and enabling prompt caching
options.C: Summarizing the preamble with the model at request time
options.D: Moving the preamble into a few-shot block

questions.rationale: A stable cached prefix cuts time-to-first-token and per-request cost together

questions.question: What belongs in an architecture decision record for a Claude system?

options.A: The final design only
options.B: The decision, the alternatives considered, the tradeoffs, and the constraints that drove the choice
options.C: The team members involved
options.D: The implementation timeline

questions.rationale: A decision record captures alternatives and tradeoffs, not just the outcome

questions.question: Observability for a production agent should capture which of the following to make incidents diagnosable?

options.A: Final outputs only
options.C: Traces of tool calls, retrieved context, and decision points alongside outputs
options.B: Aggregate latency metrics only
options.D: User feedback only

questions.rationale: Without traces of tool calls and retrieved context, failures cannot be localized to a layer

questions.question: A partner team wants to adopt your Claude Code setup. What makes adoption durable rather than a one-time handoff?

options.A: A recorded walkthrough
options.D: Version-controlled shared configuration, common skills and commands, and an onboarding path that new engineers follow
options.B: A shared chat channel
options.C: Individual coaching sessions

questions.rationale: Shared, versioned configuration with an onboarding path is what makes adoption stick

questions.question: Which change best reduces risk in an agent that can both read and modify production records?

options.B: Logging modifications for later review
options.A: Separating read and write capabilities, granting write access only where the role requires it, and gating writes behind explicit approval
options.C: Requiring a longer system prompt about caution
options.D: Running the agent during business hours only

questions.rationale: Least privilege plus approval gates on writes reduces the surface rather than monitoring it
